posts.text: I believe they let themselves be guided by old data. First waves; The old data say kids do not like LOTR so do not make sets for them and there are too few adults to sustain the theme. New waves; There is a lot more afols now and there seem to be a demand for sets, so lets take a chance and make a big sets for adults and see how well it do. It turned out to be a bestseller so lets do more of that, after a couple of years maybe try a medium set that adults might like, a book nook or a helmet bust. Future waves; Still a very long way to go before they even consider making a wave for kids again I think. However a small battle-pack sets for adults might be in reach as long as they avoid predating on the bigger sets

posts.title: Lord of the Rings Ongoing Discussion
posts.text: Seems like Lego use a lot of old data for their decisions (however now with all the financial success they seem to take more chances lately), HP is a perfect example. They released a big wave that sold very well, then another one in a non movie year that bombed (this was in the start of the HP hype and Lego was almost bankrupt at the time so this was a big deal). In the coming years as the HP hype grew every year, Lego released fewer and fewer sets for every movie, then only 1 for the 5th film and stopped. I am sure those few sets sold a lot during that time, but Lego did not dare to take any chances. Then they made a few best of sets for the last 2 films and closed down the theme since they stopped making movies. For many years Lego as a rule never made sets for a licence without it having a big movie that year. Not a bulletproof strategy since new licenced films had to be a success, films like Prince of Persia Lone and ranger had great Lego set waves, but sold poorly because the films boombed. HP was the most asked for theme (they did not have) in Lego store for many years as the HP hype kept on growing as more people red the books and watch the films. So there was a clear demand, but Lego instead looked at data from 2002. Then the FB films came and finally Lego could take the chance and release sets again. In 2018 HP had 4 of the 10 bestselling products at Lego that year (no other theme had more than 1) and here we are 8 years later with it being a evergreen theme..

posts.title: [PC] Existence of Nivo card alternative to LEGO 9771
posts.text: This thread is not about MSX, but about the NIVO-card. Let's bring the great news right away, I've found it! I even know the company that produced it, an better yet I'm still doing business with them. Let's get all the content out. NIVO stood for Nieuwe Informatietechnologie in het Voortgezet Onderwijs (“New Information Technology in Secondary Education”), a Dutch government project launched in 1984 to introduce computers and educational software into secondary schools. The interface was officially called the UIA The corresponding expansion card was the UIA: Universele Interface Adapter (“Universal Interface Adapter”). It was developed by the Centre for Microcomputer Applications, later known as CMA, the organisation behind the Coach educational measurement software. The coach software still exists and is used in secondary schools for physics measurements. The UIA was selected as the standard interface for the MS-DOS computers supplied to NIVO schools. It was a fairly sophisticated laboratory interface featuring: A 25-pin connector with digital inputs and outputs Two 8-bit parallel I/O ports Three 16-bit counters/timers with their own 1MHz clock A 9-pin connector with four analogue inputs: Two inputs with a 0–5V range Two inputs with a 0–1V range Facilities for pulse counting, timing measurements and sensor More than 500 UIA packages had reportedly been ordered at the time. The card was primarily intended for physics experiments and process control, but it could also control LEGO Interface A. See https://www.fisme.science.uu.nl/woudschotennatuurkunde/verslagen/1987-WND.pdf workgroep 24 (search for UIA) for more information about the UIA-card. In the 'Gebruikershandleiding' (usermanual) page 7 (2. Beschrijving computerset) mentions the use of a special cable only intended for the NIVO UIA card (third paragraph). The cable would be deliverd with the materialset, but its not clear to me whether that would be with the UIA-card or another set. How LEGO Lines used the card As mentioned earlier, the setup of LEGO lines uses three .DAT files. - IFlego.dat = Lego's own infterfacecard settings - IFnivo.dat = Nivo card settings (see below) - Iface.dat = config file in which the selection while setting up is saved. This is the only .DAT file Lego Lines reads. The Educaboek installation instructions contain the actual interface settings. The file IFNIVO.DAT contains: 771,139,768,770 Converted to hexadecimal: Function Decimal Hexadecimal Initialisation/control register 771 &H303 Initialisation value 139 &H8B Output address 768 &H300 Input address 770 &H302 The initialisation code on a NIVO PC was therefore effectively: OUT &H303,&H8B OUT &H300,0 Outputs were written to &H300, while the sensors were read using: A=INP(&H302) This arrangement—four consecutive I/O addresses and the configuration value &H8B—strongly indicates that the card used an Intel 8255 PPI: Port A at &H300: LEGO outputs Port B at &H301 Port C at &H302: LEGO inputs Control register at &H303 Educaboek’s preserved MS-DOS package contains both IFNIVO.DAT and IFLEGO.DAT, together with an installation program used to select the appropriate interface card. Relationship to my proposed MSX cartridge Interestingly, this confirms the approach ive been thinking about earlier: using an 8255 on an MSX cartridge. The principal difference would be the I/O address: Historical NIVO PC Possible MSX cartridge &H300–&H303 For example, &H20–&H23 PC expansion card MSX cartridge 8255 PPI 8255 PPI LEGO Lines for MS-DOS MSX BASIC or an adapted LEGO Lines I was stil typing... It's a long story as you can see. But I might contact someone at CMA now I know they've got something to do with it as well.

posts.text: Let's go... First I will try to give you guys some background on computers at school in the Netherlands based on my memory. After that I will post something you guys really will like. As some of you know I work in education as IT-manager, but my dad has been a primary school teacher. So I've watched the complete development of computers at school from nearby. <Starting the time machine.....> It's 1986/1987. At the time homecomputers are getting affordable, and you would find them at libraries and schools. The IBM/PC platform is no where to be seen other than at company's for select users. Homecomputers were mainly Commodore 64 or MSX. E.g. our library had two C64 which you could reserve time on. In my family the MSX was common, so in 1987 I got a MSX2 (shown elsewhere). At schools computers were non existant! The first computers at school were mostly Commodore 64 because a large eduction foundation (OMO = Ons Middelbaar Onderwijs) choose this. But things were changing rapidly between 88 and 91. The government aknowledged that computerknowledge was essential in the future. Therefore several 'PC-prive' projects were started to enable consumers to buy computers from their employee. As the IBM/PC was the standard in company's these projects offerd these kind of computers. Our clone pride TULIP Computers played a large role in that too. So by 1991 I got my first 386SX/25, 1Mb, 105MB hdd computer with VGA and the MSX went to the attic. This probably explains why there is proof of the C64 infertace, but not of any MSX (other than the rumour i'm researching someone has a prototype). With this in mind I will continue in the next post....
